reason: A specification whose only event never changes state -- a null detector. Design D-7 measured this hit on the frozen control and noted it would have no successor because SecretKeySpec.mop was to be deleted; D-11 withdrew that deletion and keeps all 23 files, so the hit survives with the file. It accuses nothing (no state change, no report site of its own), so leaving it costs no accusation; deleting the specification would be a change of the set's membership and belongs to whoever revisits D-11.

G-2b' flags an event whose out-alphabet at the unsafe state is a subset of the safe state's -- the idiom every `g3`/`g4`-style unsafe-getInstance event of this set uses on purpose: it records the algorithm without changing state, so the accusation lands on the call that consumes it. Design D-7 measured exactly these eight on the frozen control (CipherSpec.g3, KeyGeneratorSpec.g3, KeyManagerFactorySpec.g3, KeyPairGeneratorSpec.g3, KeyStoreSpec.g2, MacSpec.g3, MessageDigestSpec.g4, SecretKeySpec.e1) and states why the gate is a question rather than a verdict: its implied repair is absorption, which gh101 D-S9 rejected as trading a false positive for a false negative. One row for all eight, because the reason is one reason; the set is unchanged from the frozen baseline.

A redundant state in the specification D-7 already names as the set's null detector. It accuses nothing and is the same artefact as the G-2a row above, seen from the state side; it survives for the same reason (D-11 keeps the file).

The gate reads `sink = highest index` as a violation state; SecretKeySpec declares no `fail` category, so its highest-index state is not a violation state and the reading does not apply. Measured as such on the frozen control by D-7. The file survives under D-11.

Same as the SecretKeySpec row: RandomStringPasswordSpec has no `fail` category, so `sink = highest index` names no violation state. D-7 measured both; both files survive under D-11, which is why the two hits have successors where D-7 expected none.
